strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: standard on-policy distillation may inadequately preserve teacher uncertainty. The proposed remedy—adding a top-k forward-KL term at positions with high teacher entropy—is simple, intuitive, and readily compatible with existing training pipelines.

The empirical study is relatively broad. It covers three Qwen student scales, six mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, out-of-domain evaluations, and an additional Llama teacher–student pair. EOPD generally improves aggregate Avg@8 and Pass@8 over OPD, with especially notable reported Pass@8 gains for the 4B student.

The analysis includes relevant comparisons beyond the main OPD baseline: entropy bonuses, advantage shaping, full and randomly placed forward KL, threshold sensitivity, top-k probability-mass/memory tradeoffs, token-entropy histograms, and Pass@k curves.

Presentation is clear and visually polished. The motivation, algorithm, experimental settings, and major results are easy to follow, and the appendix supplies useful hyperparameters, prompt templates, and evaluation details.
The impact statement appropriately recognizes general language-model risks and makes no implausible claim of eliminating them. The work does not appear to introduce a distinct major ethical risk.
weaknesses: Soundness is the decisive concern. The toy experiment does not faithfully optimize reverse KL: it samples from a discontinuously truncated top-10 distribution and updates only the sampled logit by s_x <- s_x + eta r(x), rather than applying the full score-function gradient through the categorical softmax. Its observed top-k switching therefore does not establish that correctly optimized reverse KL is intrinsically unstable under high teacher entropy.

The central mode-collapse argument is underqualified. At each token, teacher and student softmax distributions share the full vocabulary support, and both forward and reverse KL have the same optimum when the distribution can be represented. The manuscript does not establish how its artificial top-10 capacity restriction corresponds to contextual capacity limitations in an LLM, so the toy result provides weak mechanistic support for the claimed cause of the downstream effect.

All reported model results appear to come from single training runs, with no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is particularly problematic for AIME/AMC, which have small test sets, and for sub-point Avg@8 differences. Table 2 also contains several benchmark-level regressions or ties despite the claim of consistent improvement.

Threshold tau=0.8 is selected using reported benchmark performance, apparently on the same benchmarks used for the headline evaluation, without a separate validation protocol. This creates a risk of test-set tuning. The entropy-driven and placement ablations are also limited to a subset of benchmarks and one model size.

The method description repeatedly says it selectively applies reverse KL at low entropy and forward KL at high entropy, but Equation 9 retains the reverse-KL/OPD term everywhere and adds forward KL at high-entropy positions. This distinction matters for interpreting both the mechanism and novelty.

The claimed efficiency advantage is not demonstrated. No wall-clock time, FLOPs, throughput, total teacher-query cost, or peak-memory comparison against OPD, full forward KL, KD, or GRPO is reported. Figure 10 only estimates storage for top-k values, so statements about preserving on-policy training efficiency are not adequately supported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code-release statement, seed specification, hardware configuration, dataset preprocessing/split detail, entropy-bonus coefficient, checkpoint-selection procedure, or uncertainty around evaluation. Some teacher naming is also ambiguous between “Qwen3-8B” and “Qwen3-Instruct.” These gaps would make exact reproduction difficult.

Originality is modest. Entropy-thresholded placement of a truncated forward-KL term is a natural hybrid of established forward/reverse-KL distillation ideas, and the full-forward-KL baseline is already described as a GKD variant. The paper would need stronger controlled evidence to elevate the straightforward modification into a convincing ICML contribution.

The limitations treatment is inadequate. Beyond a generic impact statement, the manuscript does not candidly discuss single-run uncertainty, benchmark-size limitations, threshold selection, dependence on access to teacher logits, or the additional computational and storage costs of entropy and top-k probability queries. Overall, the promising empirical pattern is not yet supported rigorously enough for acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The core proposal is intuitive and operationally simple: retain the on-policy reverse-KL objective and add a top-k forward-KL term at positions where teacher entropy exceeds a threshold. The paper evaluates three Qwen student sizes, an additional Llama teacher-student pair, six math benchmarks, out-of-domain tasks, and several relevant ablations.

Empirical scope: EOPD generally improves over OPD in Table 2, including reported mean Pass@8 gains of 1.37, 2.39, and 5.05 points for the 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B students. The entropy-bonus, advantage-shaping, threshold, forward-KL-placement, and top-k analyses are useful attempts to isolate the proposed mechanism.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, readable, and visually clear. The algorithm, training hyperparameters, evaluation prompts, and distinction between Avg@8 and Pass@8 are described sufficiently to understand the intended procedure.

Significance and originality: Conditioning distribution matching on teacher uncertainty is a sensible extension of on-policy distillation, and the observation that generic entropy promotion need not reproduce the teacher's uncertainty structure could be practically useful.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central toy experiment does not implement the stated reverse-KL policy gradient. It updates only the sampled logit via s_x += eta*r(x), whereas the gradient of a categorical log-softmax affects every logit. Hard top-10 sampling also introduces discontinuities that can itself cause set switching. Consequently, Figures 1 and 6 do not establish that reverse KL intrinsically becomes unstable under high teacher entropy.

Soundness: The diversity evidence is substantially confounded. Figure 3 compares model entropies on responses generated by different models, so both the model and the context distribution change; it also omits the pre-distillation student. Moreover, lower forward KL at exactly the high-entropy positions where EOPD explicitly minimizes forward KL is largely an expected training-objective result, not independent evidence that meaningful reasoning diversity was transferred. Held-out, same-context comparisons and direct trajectory-diversity or solution-diversity measurements are needed.

Evidence: No training seeds, variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the main results. This is material because several gains are small, AIME and AMC contain few questions, and EOPD loses to OPD in multiple individual cells—for example 0.6B AMC23 Pass@8, 1.7B AIME25, and 4B Minerva Avg@8. Claims of consistent improvement and training stability are therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

Claims and mechanism: The manuscript repeatedly describes selecting reverse KL for low-entropy tokens and forward KL for high-entropy tokens, but Equation 9 actually applies reverse KL everywhere and adds forward KL at high-entropy positions. It also assumes, without validating, that high token entropy represents multiple meaningful reasoning paths rather than lexical, formatting, or tokenization ambiguity. The experiments show correlation between entropy-related quantities and accuracy, not that uncertainty transfer causes the gains or is 'essential.'

Efficiency and significance: The claimed preservation of on-policy training efficiency is not demonstrated with wall-clock time, FLOPs, throughput, communication cost, or total memory. Unlike OPD, EOPD requires teacher entropy and top-k outputs at every token. Figure 10 reports only storage for top-k records, without enough setup detail, and cannot substantiate negligible overhead. The full-forward-KL baseline is already competitive in Table 6, making the practical benefit of entropy gating unclear without an end-to-end cost comparison.

Originality: The method is an incremental thresholded combination of established reverse- and forward-KL objectives, with top-k truncation. The paper itself notes that full placement resembles GKD. The limited mechanistic validation and absence of a clear efficiency advantage leave the originality and broader significance below the acceptance bar.

Reproducibility: There is no code or artifact availability statement, and important information remains unclear, including exact teacher checkpoint identity, number of optimization steps and checkpoint selection, hardware and numerical precision, dataset preprocessing, evaluation randomness, seed policy, and end-to-end cost. The appendix also states that different chat templates are used for distillation and GRPO, weakening comparisons against that baseline.

Limitations and ethics: The impact statement appropriately identifies no distinctive new ethical risk, but the paper lacks a substantive limitations discussion. It should address dependence on access to teacher logits, entropy-threshold calibration across tokenizers and teachers, semantic ambiguity of token entropy, increased training overhead, benchmark contamination, and uncertainty in automatic grading. The claimed environmental benefit is speculative because compute and energy costs are not measured.

strengths: Soundness: The central intervention is technically plausible and easy to understand: EOPD retains clipped reverse-KL on-policy distillation while adding a top-k forward-KL term at positions where teacher entropy exceeds a threshold. Comparisons with entropy bonuses, advantage shaping, random placement, and full forward-KL help isolate the value of teacher-conditioned uncertainty guidance.

Evaluation: Results span three Qwen student scales, six mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, several out-of-domain benchmarks, and an additional Llama teacher-student pair. Relative to OPD, the average gains are meaningful, especially the reported Pass@8 gains of 2.39 points for Qwen3-1.7B and 5.05 points for Qwen3-4B.

Analysis: The paper connects downstream gains to relevant distributional measurements. EOPD preserves more high-entropy tokens and attains lower forward KL to the teacher at uncertain positions; increasing Pass@k advantages provide further evidence that it preserves useful diversity rather than merely increasing single-sample accuracy.

Presentation: The motivation, equations, algorithm, experimental questions, and ablations are organized clearly. The appendices provide useful training hyperparameters, prompt templates, evaluation settings, top-k memory analysis, and additional model-family results.

Significance and originality: Entropy-gated placement of forward KL is an incremental but useful refinement of on-policy distillation. It addresses a practically relevant failure mode with modest conceptual and implementation complexity.
Ethics: The impact statement appropriately discusses efficiency and acknowledges general language-model risks. The method does not appear to introduce a distinctive unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The toy experiment does not convincingly establish the broad claim that reverse-KL gradients are inherently unstable under high teacher entropy. Its update changes only the sampled logit and imposes a discontinuous top-10 sampling restriction, unlike the full softmax policy-gradient update used for an LLM; these choices can themselves produce changing top-k sets. The paper should distinguish this constructed capacity-restricted behavior from a general property of reverse-KL optimization.

Statistical evidence is limited. Results appear to come from single training runs, with no seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This matters because several test sets are small and many gains are modest or mixed: EOPD loses to OPD on some individual Avg@8 or Pass@8 entries, despite claims of consistent improvement.

The diversity analysis is partly ambiguous. It is not clearly stated whether teacher, OPD, and EOPD entropies in Figure 3 are measured on identical contexts; entropy histograms over each model's separately generated trajectories confound conditional-distribution alignment with differences in visited contexts. Lower forward KL in Figure 5 is also an expected consequence of directly optimizing that quantity and is not independently sufficient to establish better reasoning-path diversity.

The evidence for entropy-aware placement over simpler forward-KL augmentation is suggestive rather than decisive. Full forward KL is competitive in Table 6 and even wins AIME25 Pass@8, while comparisons cover only four benchmarks and one student size without uncertainty estimates. Consequently, the incremental benefit of thresholding is less firmly established than the benefit of adding forward KL itself.

The claim of retaining on-policy training efficiency is unsupported by wall-clock time, FLOPs, throughput, peak memory, or teacher-query cost comparisons. Computing teacher entropy and top-k probabilities is more demanding than obtaining only sampled-token log-probabilities; Figure 10 reports storage cost but not end-to-end overhead.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful appendix details: there is no code-release statement, seed information, hardware or training-time report, exact update/step counts, complete GRPO configuration, entropy-bonus coefficient, or sufficiently precise checkpoint and preprocessing specifications. These omissions make exact replication and fair compute comparison difficult.

Limitations are not discussed explicitly enough. The paper should acknowledge dependence on access to teacher logits, threshold and vocabulary/tokenizer assumptions, the narrow emphasis on mathematical reasoning, single-teacher settings, and the absence of statistical and compute-cost validation. The broad conclusion that modeling teacher uncertainty is 'essential' therefore overstates the current evidence.

strengths: Soundness: EOPD is technically plausible and simple: it augments clipped reverse-KL on-policy distillation with a top-k forward-KL term when teacher token entropy exceeds a threshold. The manuscript evaluates three Qwen student sizes, an additional Llama teacher–student pair, six math benchmarks, three out-of-domain evaluations, and several relevant baselines.

Evidence: Across the six math benchmarks, EOPD improves mean Avg@8/Pass@8 over OPD by +1.16/+1.37, +0.99/+2.39, and +1.80/+5.05 for the 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B Qwen students, respectively. Comparisons against entropy bonuses, advantage shaping, GKD, full/random forward-KL placement, and adaptive-KL methods help isolate the proposed design.

Significance: Selective forward KL is a useful practical compromise. The reported implementation adds about 4.5% training time and 219.3 MB memory, versus 1617.5 MB for forward KL at every position, while generally matching or improving full-forward-KL performance.

Analysis: The entropy histograms, high-entropy-region forward-KL curves, forward-KL placement controls, and threshold/coefficient/top-k ablations provide mutually relevant evidence that teacher-guided distribution matching is more useful than merely increasing policy entropy.

Presentation and reproducibility: The method, pseudocode, objectives, prompts, training and evaluation settings, model families, hardware, and principal hyperparameters are mostly documented clearly. The paper is readable and the appendix is substantial.

Originality: Teacher-entropy-gated forward KL within on-policy language-model distillation is an intuitive but meaningful synthesis, even though adaptive divergence selection and entropy-aware training already have close precedents.
Ethics: The impact statement appropriately discusses efficiency and general language-model risks; the work does not appear to introduce a distinct material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central toy experiment does not faithfully implement the stated reverse-KL policy gradient. It updates only the sampled logit via s_x += eta*r(x), omitting the softmax policy-gradient effects on all logits, and restricts sampling to the current top 10. Its top-k and top-1 change statistics can also fluctuate naturally for a high-entropy distribution with nearly tied probabilities. Without comparison to the true reverse-KL gradient, forward KL, or final KL error, this experiment does not establish that reverse KL itself produces unstable optimization signals.

Soundness: The headline entropy-collapse comparison is confounded. Section 3.1 computes teacher entropy on teacher-generated responses and student entropy on student-generated responses, so the reported 18.5% versus 6.8% high-entropy-token rates mix model-distribution differences with different generated contexts. A compelling transfer analysis should evaluate teacher and student distributions on identical contexts and report calibrated divergence or coverage measures.

Statistical evidence: Results appear to be single runs with no training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several gains are small or inconsistent—for example, EOPD is below OPD on Qwen-1.7B AIME25 Avg@8 and Qwen-4B Minerva Avg@8—and AIME has only 30 questions, making Pass@8 changes very coarse. The evidence therefore does not justify claims of consistently better or more stable performance.

Evaluation methodology: The paper says the final threshold tau=0.8, coefficient alpha=1.0, and top-k=16 were selected because they perform best in ablations on MATH500, AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25, which are also reported as test benchmarks. No separate validation protocol is described, creating a substantial risk of test-set hyperparameter selection.

Causal claims remain too strong: Better Pass@k is attributed to more diverse reasoning trajectories, but only token entropy and outcome accuracy are measured. There is no semantic or reasoning-path diversity analysis, and higher entropy need not imply useful trajectory diversity. Likewise, lower forward KL is partly a direct consequence of explicitly optimizing forward KL and is not independent validation of the proposed mechanism.

Baseline fairness and completeness are insufficiently documented. GRPO uses a different chat template and eight training rollouts per prompt, while distillation uses one; reward construction and total token/compute budgets are not fully specified. Entropy-bonus implementation details omit its objective coefficient. These choices hinder controlled comparison.

Reproducibility: Exact checkpoint identifiers are ambiguous—the text alternates between “Qwen3-8B” and “Qwen3-Instruct”—and the number of optimizer steps, dataset preprocessing, random seeds, evaluation seed handling, decoding repetitions, and full baseline hyperparameter tuning are missing. The abstract states that code is public but provides no usable location in the manuscript.

Originality is incremental relative to the cited BD-KD, AKL, ToDi, GKD, and entropy-aware exploration literature. The paper demonstrates a useful engineering rule, but offers no theoretical characterization of when entropy thresholding should be preferred or how the threshold should scale across teachers, temperatures, or vocabularies.

Presentation: The paper repeatedly describes EOPD as using reverse KL in low-entropy regions and forward KL in high-entropy regions, but Equation 9 retains the reverse-KL term everywhere and adds forward KL at high-entropy positions. The wording should reflect this additive objective. The reported selective-forward-KL memory is also inconsistent: 219.3 MB in Appendix A versus 144 MiB in the top-k analysis.

strengths: The proposed entropy-gated combination of reverse and forward KL is simple, intuitive, and readily implementable. Applying top-k forward KL only at uncertain positions is a potentially useful memory/quality tradeoff.

The empirical study is broad: three Qwen student sizes, an additional Llama experiment, six math benchmarks, out-of-domain evaluations, adaptive-KL and entropy-promoting baselines, and ablations over the threshold, coefficient, and top-k.
The paper reports practical costs, including training-time overhead and memory usage, and provides substantially more implementation detail than many LLM post-training papers.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with readable algorithms, tables, and appendices. The limitations of truncated forward KL and the method's additional overhead are at least partly investigated.
The impact statement appropriately recognizes general language-model risks, and I found no material new ethical concern specific to the method.
weaknesses: Soundness: the toy experiment does not implement the policy-gradient optimization used by OPD. It updates only the sampled logit via s_x <- s_x + eta r(x), omitting the softmax policy-gradient term that changes every logit. Its hard top-10 sampling restriction also creates discontinuities that can itself cause set churn. Consequently, Figures 1 and 6 do not substantiate the central claim that reverse-KL policy gradients become intrinsically unstable under high teacher entropy.

Soundness: the main LLM experiments appear to use one training run per configuration and report neither seed variation nor confidence intervals. Many claimed improvements are small, while AIME has only 30 questions and several Pass@8 entries differ by one or two questions. Without uncertainty estimates or paired tests, the evidence does not establish that the gains are reliable.

The causal account is inadequately tested. Token entropy can reflect lexical, formatting, or local syntactic alternatives rather than distinct reasoning paths. The paper provides no semantic analysis of high-entropy positions and no direct measurement of solution-path diversity. Higher Pass@k is only indirect evidence and can also arise from ordinary accuracy changes.

The entropy histogram comparison is confounded because teacher, OPD, and EOPD entropies are measured on model-generated trajectories, hence generally on different contexts. A controlled comparison on identical contexts is needed before concluding that EOPD better transfers teacher uncertainty.

Lower forward KL on high-teacher-entropy tokens is largely a training-objective diagnostic: EOPD explicitly minimizes that quantity at those positions. It is not independent validation of the proposed mechanism.

The entropy-aware routing itself is not convincingly separated from simply adding more distillation supervision. Full forward KL is statistically indistinguishable from EOPD in Table 7 and even has higher AIME25 Pass@8; the manuscript provides no replicated quality-versus-total-memory comparison to establish the claimed advantage. The reported 7.37x figure concerns additional tensors rather than overall peak memory.

Equation 10 is a biased truncated objective, not simply the full forward KL: the teacher is renormalized over its top-k support while the student is not. Aggregate top-k mass is reported, but truncation error specifically at the selected high-entropy positions—the regime where tails should matter most—is not quantified.

Originality is modest. Entropy-conditioned divergence selection is a straightforward adaptive-KL heuristic, and the related-work section itself identifies prior methods that adapt KL using entropy gaps or other teacher-student discrepancies. The paper does not provide a formal result or sufficiently rigorous empirical mechanism study to elevate the conceptual novelty.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract ends with “Our code is publicly available at” but supplies no URL. Important details such as LLM-run seeds, PPO clipping epsilon, some baseline coefficients/reward specifications, checkpoint-selection procedure, and complete preprocessing are absent. Public model and framework names plus several hyperparameter tables help, but are insufficient for exact reproduction.

Presentation overstates the findings: phrases such as “demonstrate,” “essential,” and “stable” are not warranted by single-run results, a flawed toy proxy, and diagnostic measurements partly optimized by construction. The paper also alternates between describing EOPD as replacing reverse KL at high-entropy positions and, correctly according to Equation 9, adding forward KL while retaining reverse KL there.

strengths: Soundness: The core proposal is intuitive and technically plausible: EOPD augments clipped reverse-KL on-policy distillation with top-k forward KL specifically at contexts where teacher entropy exceeds a threshold.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a distillation paper, covering three Qwen student scales, six mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, out-of-domain tasks, and an additional Llama teacher-student pair.

The experiments consistently favor EOPD over standard OPD on aggregate. The reported Pass@8 gains over OPD increase with student scale (+1.37, +2.39, and +5.05 points), while the token-entropy and forward-KL analyses support the intended mechanism.

The ablations and controls are valuable: the paper compares full, random, and entropy-conditioned forward-KL placement; forward- versus reverse-KL OPD; entropy bonuses; advantage shaping; GKD; and several adaptive-distillation baselines. Sensitivity analyses for the entropy threshold, forward-KL weight, and top-k truncation further strengthen the evidence.

Significance and originality: Although the method is simple and related to prior adaptive-divergence approaches, using teacher entropy to route token-level KL objectives in on-policy LLM distillation is a useful contribution. The approximately 4.5% reported training-time overhead makes the technique practically relevant.

Presentation: The manuscript is clearly organized, explains the motivation and algorithm well, and includes informative tables and figures. The rendered manuscript is generally polished and legible. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d24502b7148f4155ad56342a0280f346/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The impact discussion identifies no method-specific ethical risk, which is reasonable for this work, and notes possible computational benefits from deploying smaller models.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim is stronger than the evidence. The toy experiment uses top-10-restricted sampling and a nonstandard update that changes only the sampled logit. Its persistent top-k churn may arise from this estimator and truncation rather than an inherent instability of reverse KL under high teacher entropy. Exact reverse-KL minimization itself has the teacher distribution as its optimum in the unrestricted setting.

The paper repeatedly interprets high token entropy as meaningful diversity or multiple reasoning paths, but entropy can also reflect lexical variation, formatting, or teacher uncertainty/error. The evidence shows distributional alignment and higher Pass@k, not that EOPD preserves semantically distinct valid reasoning trajectories. A trajectory-level diversity or correctness-conditioned analysis is missing.

The evaluation lacks repeated training runs, uncertainty intervals, or statistical tests for the main LLM experiments. Several gains occur on very small benchmarks such as AIME, where one problem can materially change Pass@8, and EOPD also has individual regressions. Consequently, the consistency and magnitude of the improvement are less certain than the prose suggests.

Hyperparameter selection may use evaluation benchmarks directly: the threshold, forward-KL coefficient, and top-k ablations report MATH500, AMC23, and AIME performance, and the best settings are then used in the main results. No separate validation protocol is described, creating a risk of test-set tuning.

The comparison with full forward KL weakens the claimed necessity of entropy-aware routing: full forward KL is often tied with or close to EOPD and even has higher AIME25 Pass@8. The strongest demonstrated advantage of routing is therefore efficiency plus modest aggregate performance, rather than an unequivocally superior learning objective.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite substantial implementation detail. The manuscript does not report seeds for full training, PPO clipping and several optimizer settings, exact checkpoint identifiers consistently, training step counts, baseline-specific tuning budgets, or a usable anonymized code artifact. There is also an inconsistency between describing the teacher as Qwen3-8B and as Qwen3-Instruct in the appendix.

Scope and limitations are underdeveloped. Most evidence concerns mathematics, only one additional model family is tested, and all teachers are around 8B parameters. The paper has no dedicated limitations discussion addressing threshold calibration, dependence on teacher entropy quality, applicability to non-reasoning domains, or the extra storage and access required for teacher top-k distributions.

The impact statement is acceptable but generic; it does not discuss inherited teacher biases or the possibility that matching uncertain teacher distributions also transfers teacher errors. These are not blocking ethical concerns, but they should be acknowledged.
